questions.q: State the formula that relates Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA), nutrient requirement, and margin of safety as given in the NCERT textbook.
questions.a: RDA = Requirement + Margin of safety. A wrong answer (e.g., "RDA = Requirement" or "RDA = Requirement × Safety factor") reveals the student has memorised the term but not the additive relationship explicitly stated in the textbook, leading to errors in explaining why RDA exceeds the average need.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the RDA for a nutrient is set higher than the average physiological requirement for that nutrient.
questions.a: The average requirement meets the need of only 50% of healthy individuals; the safety margin covers inter-individual variation in absorption, metabolism, and utilisation so that 97-98% of the population is covered. A wrong answer focusing only on "extra for safety" without mentioning population coverage or variability shows incomplete understanding of the statistical basis of RDA.

questions.q: A 16-year-old sedentary boy (ICMR reference weight 55 kg) consumes 45 g protein daily. The ICMR 2020 RDA for protein for his category is 0.83 g/kg body weight. Does his intake meet the RDA? Show your calculation.
questions.a: RDA = 0.83 g/kg × 55 kg = 45.65 g/day. His intake (45 g) is slightly below RDA. A student who calculates 0.83 × 55 = 45.65 but says "yes, it meets" reveals inability to interpret "meeting RDA" as ≥ RDA, not ≈ RDA. Another common error: using 1 g/kg (old ICMR value) instead of 0.83 g/kg.

questions.q: Compare the purpose of "Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)" and "Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)" in diet planning. Why would a public health nutritionist use EAR for assessing population intake adequacy but RDA for planning individual diets?
questions.a: EAR is the median requirement (meets 50% of population); used to estimate prevalence of inadequacy in groups. RDA = EAR + 2 SD (covers 97-98%); used for individual planning to ensure near-certain adequacy. A wrong answer confusing the two purposes (e.g., using RDA for population assessment) shows failure to grasp the probabilistic nature of these reference values — a key board exam distinction.

questions.q: Critique this statement: "Since RDA includes a safety margin, consuming exactly the RDA amount of a nutrient every day guarantees that an individual will not develop a deficiency."
questions.a: The statement is flawed. RDA covers 97-98% of healthy individuals; 2-3% may have higher needs due to genetic/metabolic factors. Also, RDA assumes normal absorption; illness, parasites, or drug interactions can increase needs beyond RDA. A student who agrees without qualification shows misunderstanding of "covers nearly all" vs. "guarantees for every individual" — a nuance examiners test via "justify your answer" questions.

questions.q: Design a one-day vegetarian menu for a 14-year-old girl (reference weight 48 kg, moderate activity) that meets at least 90% of ICMR 2020 RDAs for energy, protein, iron, and calcium. List food items with raw weights and show the nutrient calculation for one nutrient of your choice.
questions.a: Sample menu: Breakfast — 60 g wheat flour (chapati), 30 g besan (chilla), 100 ml milk; Lunch — 80 g rice, 30 g moong dal, 100 g spinach, 50 g curd; Snack — 20 g roasted chana, 50 g guava; Dinner — 60 g wheat flour, 30 g rajma, 100 g pumpkin, 50 g curd. Iron calculation: chapati (60 g × 3.9 mg/100g = 2.34) + besan (30 g × 4.9 = 1.47) + rice (80 g × 0.7 = 0.56) + moong (30 g × 3.8 = 1.14) + spinach (100 g × 2.7 = 2.7) + chana (20 g × 5.3 = 1.06) + rajma (30 g × 5.1 = 1.53) = 10.8 mg. RDA for girl 13-15 yr = 28 mg; 10.8/28 = 39% — reveals need for more iron-rich foods. A poor answer omits raw weights, uses cooked weights, or picks a nutrient without showing the full computation chain.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) are the estimated nutrient intake levels that meet the requirements of nearly all (97-98%) healthy individuals in a specific life-stage and gender group, ______ a margin of safety above the average physiological requirement to account for individual variability in absorption and utilisation.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ a week's tiffin for your 15-year-old sister who plays badminton daily.
What is Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) are the estimated nutrient intake levels that meet the requirements of nearly all (97-98%) healthy individuals in a specific life-stage and gender group, incorporating a margin of safety above the average physiological requirement to account for individual variability in absorption and utilisation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are planning a week's tiffin for your ______-year-old sister who plays badminton daily.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs)?
questions.a: Students treat RDA as the "exact daily need" for a specific person and believe eating exactly the RDA value guarantees adequacy.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly differentiate between nutrient requirement and RDA, explain why a safety margin is added, and use ICMR RDA tables to evaluate whether a given day's diet meets the allowances for a specific adolescent profile.
